summary: Indiana's pierhead light at the end of Michigan City's east pier: a 1904 steel tower and elevated walk, a shore keeper's house kept until 1940, and a 1913 storm that took the walk.

lens.where: original 1904 fifth-order Fresnel; by 1984 an American Rotating Beacon plastic lens was in the lantern (NRHP nomination)

structures.note: Steel octagonal tower on the steel fog-signal building (brick-lined); 49 ft 6 in from base to outer ventilator ball of lantern (cite 1)
24 ft square; housed two boilers operating a 10-inch Crosby automatic whistle (cite 1, 4)
About 600 ft to a 37-degree bend on a concrete pier about 1,100 ft long; original walk section destroyed in 1913 and 1929 storms (cite 1, 4, 6)

access.note: The city's visitor page presents the pier as a public fishing and sunset spot. LighthouseFriends' visitor notes say 'Tower closed.' The USLHS record says 'Open to Public: No' for the light.

facts.agency: City of Michigan City (awarded after the Coast Guard declared the light excess in 2007, per LighthouseFriends). Earlier operator: U.S. Coast Guard, from 1939 (city visitor page) or 1940 (NRHP nomination).

events.note: Fog-signal building, octagonal tower and elevated walk completed as part of the 1904 harbor improvements
Fixed white light moved from the 1858 shore house to the outer end of the east pier on 20 October 1904
Original fifth-order Fresnel lens (USLHS record)
Ten-inch steam whistle in the fog-signal building
Storm of 8-10 November 1913
About 200 ft of the elevated walk destroyed; keepers used an aerial trolley with a breeches buoy to cross the gap (LighthouseFriends)
Keeper Thomas J. Armstrong rescued two men caught at the end of the breakwater during a squall, 14 July 1915
First assistant Thomas E. Martin rescued a man and a boy from probable drowning, 13 August 1916
Keeper Thomas J. Armstrong rescued a boy who had gone overboard from the dock near the light, 15 August 1916
Storm of 18-19 December 1929 carried away the outermost 312 ft of the elevated walkway
Piers given new concrete superstructures in 1930-31 after the 1929 storm
Light electrified (NRHP nomination; city visitor page)
LighthouseFriends says the light was automated in 1933; the NRHP nomination and city page say electrified. The sources disagree on whether keepers stayed on until 1940
Coast Guard took over the lighthouse service (city visitor page); the NRHP nomination dates Coast Guard jurisdiction from 1940
Keepers ceased living in the 1858 house; keeper Walter A. Donovan died in 1940 (LighthouseFriends)
Light operated remotely by electronic equipment installed 1982-83
Building sandblasted, patched, primed and painted; new interior wiring and modernized radio beacon installed
Catwalk turned over to Michigan City
Coast Guard declared the light excess (May 2007); Michigan City filed interest and was eventually awarded the light
Repainted and refurbished in a $160,000 project

corrections.proposed: 1904 first_lit (light moved to the outer end of the east pier, 20 October 1904)
corrections.why: LighthouseFriends describes an 1871 wooden pierhead tower and elevated walk on the east pier, moved to the west pier in 1875. The lit date for the present structure is 1904 (NRHP nomination; USLHS establishment year).
The 1984 NRHP nomination gives the focal plane as 43 feet. Check against the current Coast Guard Light List before changing the record.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1871 date in the record belongs to an earlier wooden pierhead tower on the east pier, later moved to the west pier. The present light was first shown from the east pier on 20 October 1904.

The USLHS record says the light is not an active aid to navigation, but the city describes it as a public operating lighthouse and the 1984 nomination describes it as used by sport and commercial fishermen. The current status is treated as active, subject to confirmation.

The NRHP nomination and the city page say electrified in 1933. LighthouseFriends says automated in 1933. Both can be true if electrification came first and remote operation later, but the sources do not say so.

notes_for_editor: Roster: the USLHS place page matched by name; its position is about 1.2 km from the record's OSM position (USLHS positions are only to the minute), so the roster is for the same pierhead light but the match is by name. Roster lines are quoted as printed. 'Frederick Dykeman' in the roster is 'Fred Dykeman' in the 1916 Bulletin; treated as the same man because the Bulletin calls him second assistant. The 1904 construction and lighting rest on the NRHP nomination and LighthouseFriends; the Lighthouse Board's 1904 report and the Michigan City Evening News items the nomination cites are not in the corpus, and Chronicling America returned HTTP 520 for one 1904 search (retried) and no hits for two others. The USCG Historian's archived page for this light returned nothing usable (blocked or empty capture), so it is not cited. The 1913 and 1916 Bulletin passages are OCR text; quotes avoid the garbled words ('ab out', 'Oity', 'Micbigan', 'l'escued'). Harriet Colfax is in the keepers list from LighthouseFriends only; she was the keeper of the 1858 shore light, which the East Pierhead light was moved from; there is also a separate record for the 1858 light (us-in-michigan-city-old). The 1984 NRHP nomination is the only long source on the structure; no current Coast Guard source was read, so the status and ownership lines rest on the city page and LighthouseFriends. LighthouseFriends attributes an 1974 NRHP listing to both the 1858 house and the pier; the nomination's reference number (88000069) points to 1988 per the record, which I did not confirm from a source read. Checked 2026-10-22: the $5,500 fog-signal money came from the sundry civil appropriation act approved 6 June 1900 (Board report, scan p.167), not a harbor act; LighthouseFriends' visitor notes say 'Tower closed.', which the story now reports. The Colfax 1861-1904 span is LighthouseFriends' (she is not on the USLHS roster).
